papers.title: Fishing for new immunotherapy compounds to boost innate tumor rejection
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766748 v1

summary.one_liner: A zebrafish xenograft phenotypic screen of over 500 FDA-approved drugs identified tiotropium bromide, a muscarinic antagonist, which reprograms tumor-associated macrophages and synergizes with anti-PD-1 in a syngeneic CT26 mouse model.
summary.plain: Some tumors are cleared by the immune system when transplanted into zebrafish, while others take hold. The authors screened hundreds of approved drugs for ones that help the fish's innate immune system clear human colorectal and breast cancer cells. They report that tiotropium, an inhaled asthma and COPD drug, stood out, and that it works through immune cells called macrophages.
summary.why: It suggests a route to drug repurposing for immunotherapy resistance and points to the nervous system's influence on immunity as a possible target. The text reports mouse results with anti-PD-1 but does not show clinical use, so the translational value is still unproven.
summary.background:
- Innate immunity is the body's first-line, non-specific defense, including macrophages that engulf (phagocytose) cells.
- Zebrafish xenografts: human tumor cells transplanted into young zebrafish, which are transparent and allow fast in vivo imaging.
- Phenotypic screen: testing many compounds by their observable effect (here, tumor clearance) without knowing the target beforehand.
- Muscarinic receptors are nerve-signal receptors that respond to acetylcholine; antagonists block them.
- Anti-PD-1 is an immune checkpoint antibody that releases the brakes on T cells.
- CT26 is a mouse colon tumor line; NSG mice lack functional immune cells, so the drug's effect disappearing there implies immune involvement.
- Results so far come from preclinical models (fish and mice), not human patients.

papers.abstract: Despite significant advances in cancer immunotherapy, tackling immunosuppression remains critical to achieve more effective responses. While developing the zebrafish xenograft model, we found that some human tumors engraft very efficiently ("progressors"), while others are cleared by the host ("regressors"). We showed that this was dependent on innate immunity, which recognizes and eliminates some cancer cells, while others are able to evade and suppress it. This opened an opportunity to perform an in vivo phenotypic drug screen to find compounds that induce clearance by boosting innate-tumor rejection. Zebrafish xenografts of human colorectal (CRC) and breast cancer (BC) that show a high engraftment/low clearance phenotype were used to screen over 500 FDA-approved small-molecule compounds, with tumor clearance serving as the phenotypic readout. The screen identified 23 hit compounds, of which six were effective across both cancer models. Mechanism-of-action enrichment analysis revealed a significant overrepresentation of autonomic nervous system-targeting drugs among the hits, particularly cholinergic ones. Immune profiling in myeloid reporter lines showed that the lead hit, Tiotropium bromide, a muscarinic receptor antagonist, reprograms tumor-associated macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory, anti-tumoral state. Tiotropium significantly increased macrophage phagocytosis, and macrophage depletion completely abolished its pro-clearance activity, establishing these myeloid cells as essential effectors. In a syngeneic CT26 colorectal mouse model, Tiotropium synergized with anti-PD-1 to control tumor growth and improve survival, outperforming all monotherapy arms. This effect was immune-dependent, as it was lost in immunodeficient NSG mice. Together, these findings demonstrate that in vivo phenotypic screening of FDA-approved compounds in zebrafish xenografts is a productive strategy for innate immune drug discovery in cancer. The identification of Tiotropium as a myeloid-reprogramming innate immune primer, together with the unbiased recovery of the neuro-immune axis as a druggable target, opens new avenues for overcoming immunotherapy resistance.

papers.title: Beyond IgG: Oral Secretory IgA as a new efficient modality for cancer immunotherapy
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.768496 v1

summary.one_liner: A preclinical study in mice testing an orally delivered, mucosal-type secretory IgA antibody against CEACAM5 in colorectal and gastric cancer models, compared with an IgG1 version and cetuximab, alone and with chemotherapy.
summary.plain: Most cancer antibody drugs are given by injection into the bloodstream. This paper tests whether an antibody taken by mouth, in a form normally found in the gut lining (secretory IgA), can reach colorectal tumors and their spread to other sites and slow them down. In mouse models, the oral antibody (called ABC-101) concentrated in CEACAM5-positive tumors while staying at low levels in the rest of the body, and it did better than the comparison antibodies in slowing tumor growth and spread.
summary.why: If an oral antibody can work safely and selectively, it could offer a non-injected option for cancer treatment and a new way to use the immune system's mucosal defenses. The text reports only mouse experiments, so whether any of this carries over to people is unknown.
summary.background:
- Antibodies: immune proteins that bind a specific target; most cancer antibody drugs are IgG and given intravenously.
- Secretory IgA (SIgA): the antibody type the body uses on mucosal surfaces such as the gut; it is more resistant to digestion than IgG.
- CEACAM5: a protein often found at high levels on colorectal and gastric cancer cells, used here as the target.
- Cetuximab: an approved antibody drug used as a comparison.
- FOLFIRI and irinotecan: standard chemotherapy regimens for colorectal cancer.
- FcRI (CD89): a receptor on certain immune cells (neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells) that the authors say the antibody helps recruit.
- Orthotopic model: human cancer cells implanted in the organ where the cancer naturally arises, in mice.
- Preclinical: tested in cells and animals, not yet in people.

papers.abstract: Monoclonal antibody therapies have revolutionized cancer treatment but are almost exclusively based on intravenously administered IgG antibodies. Here, we developed and evaluated the first orally delivered anti-CEACAM5 secretory IgA (SIgA) for colorectal cancer. The pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, antitumor efficacy and immune effects of oral anti-CEACAM5 SIgA (ABC-101) were evaluated in an orthotopic metastatic human colorectal cancer model. Its therapeutic activity was compared with cetuximab, as monotherapy and in combination with irinotecan- or FOLFIRI-based chemotherapy along with that of an anti-CEACAM5 IgG1 sharing the same antigen-binding domain. Tumor-associated FcRI (CD89)-expressing myeloid populations were characterized at primary and metastatic sites. ABC-101 activity was evaluated on a second human cancer cell line, in vivo in an orthotopic human gastric cancer model. Oral anti-CEACAM5 SIgA (ABC-101) exhibited a unique pharmacokinetic profile, selectively accumulating in CEACAM5-positive primary tumors and metastases while maintaining minimal systemic exposure. Compared with the anti-CEACAM5 IgG1 and cetuximab, oral SIgA achieved superior inhibition of primary tumor growth and metastatic dissemination. It also enhanced the efficacy of irinotecan- and FOLFIRI-based chemotherapy, outperforming the FOLFIRI/cetuximab standard-of-care comparator. Mechanistically, ABC-101 remodeled the tumor immune microenvironment by promoting the recruitment of FcRI (CD89)-expressing neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells at both primary and metastatic sites, consistent with enhanced innate antitumor activity. Oral ABC-101 shows targeted activity against CEAhigh MKN-45 cells, reducing markers of cell proliferation and migration. These findings establish therapeutic SIgA as a first-in-class oral antibody immunotherapy combining selective tumor targeting, innate immune activation, and enhanced chemotherapy efficacy. More broadly, this work establishes mucosal immunity as a promising therapeutic frontier, demonstrating that orally delivered antibodies can enable systemic control of metastatic digestive cancers.

papers.title: Media matters: A resource for understanding the determinants of migratory potential of malignant and non-malignant cells
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767665 v1

summary.background:
- Migration/invasion assay: a lab test where cells close a scratch or gap in a dish, or push through a barrier, and researchers measure how fast they do so.
- Malignant vs non-malignant cells: cancerous cells versus normal cells taken from the same kind of tissue.
- Glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation: two ways cells turn sugar into energy, one without oxygen and one using the mitochondria.
- Metastasis: the spread of cancer from its original site to other organs.
- Migrastatic/antimetastatic therapy: drugs meant to slow cell movement or spread rather than kill the tumour cells directly.
- Culture media: the nutrient liquid cells grow in; this paper varied serum, calcium and glucose levels.
summary.one_liner: A high-throughput wound-healing/invasion screen of more than 60 malignant and non-malignant cell lines from six tissues, probing how glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, and culture media affect migration and metastatic potential.
summary.plain: Cells move around the body to heal wounds, and cancer cells move to spread tumours to new organs. This paper tested dozens of normal and cancer cell lines from the pancreas, colon, skin, breast, prostate and lung to see how fast each kind moves and invades. It found that normal lung, skin and pancreas cells often moved faster than their cancer counterparts, and that the nutrient mix in the culture liquid changed how cancer cells behaved.
summary.why: Cell movement is central to both cancer spread and wound healing, and the authors argue that few migration-targeting drugs have reached clinical trials. The screen is offered as a reference resource, and the link to new drug targets is a proposal in the text rather than a demonstrated result.

papers.abstract: Cell mobility is critical for homeostatic processes such as wound repair and diseases like cancer metastasis. While the advent of migrastatic and antimetastatic therapies has promise, the identification and translation of pathways important for migratory plasticity into druggable targets approved in clinical trials are considerably lacking. To better understand why, we developed an unbiased high-throughput wound-healing/invasion assay to screen for the migratory potential of >60 non-malignant and malignant cell lines derived from the pancreas, colon, skin, breast, prostate, and lung. The goal of this phenotypic screen was to provide a resource of migration/invasion potential and insight into the differential properties not only between malignant and non-malignant cells but also the various carcinomas. Surprisingly, we found non-malignant epithelial cells of the lung, skin, and pancreas migrated/invaded faster than their malignant counterparts. We observed perturbation of glucose metabolism, via inhibition of glycolysis, restricted the migration of non-malignant but not cancer cells, whereas inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation limited the mobility of malignant more than normal cells of the lung, skin, and pancreas. Short-term acclimation of cancer cells in low-nutrient media, containing low/no serum, low calcium, and physiological concentrations of glucose, increased in vitro migration/invasion and in vivo metastatic potential of lung but not pancreatic carcinomas. Phenotypic and metabolic screens presented here could identify prospective therapeutics not only for cancer metastasis, but also diseases driven by the dysregulation of wound-healing/regeneration.

papers.title: Metabolic priming recruits tumour cells across a mitochondrial vulnerability threshold and sensitizes them to chemotherapy
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766410 v1

summary.background:
- Intratumour heterogeneity: cancer cells within one tumour differ, so some survive treatment.
- Mitochondria: small structures that produce cell energy; their membrane voltage matters for cell survival.
- TMRM: a fluorescent dye that accumulates in mitochondria depending on membrane voltage and can act as a photosensitizer (light-activated damage agent) producing reactive oxygen species.
- Photodynamic damage: killing cells with light plus a light-sensitive agent.
- PKM2 and TEPP46: PKM2 is an enzyme in energy metabolism; TEPP46 is a drug that activates it.
- Camptothecin and TRAIL: an anticancer drug and a cell-death signalling protein, used here in combination tests.
- Bliss independence: a standard expected-effect model for combined treatments; survival below this expectation suggests synergy.
- AUC (area under the ROC curve): a 0.5 score is chance and 1.0 is perfect prediction.
summary.one_liner: Single-cell study showing that metabolic priming (TEPP46, ethyl pyruvate, camptothecin) can push a subset of cancer cells into a transient mitochondrial state that responds to TMRM-based photodynamic damage, with descriptors of the fluorescence response predicting cell fate.
summary.plain: Cancer tumours contain mixed populations of cells, and some survive treatments that kill most of the others. This paper asks whether drugs that shift cells' energy metabolism can move a fraction of them into a fragile state in their mitochondria (the cell's energy-producing parts) that is more easily damaged by light-activated dye. The authors tracked the dye's glow in individual cells and found that a measure relative to each cell's own resting level predicted whether the cell would die.
summary.why: It proposes a way to find and follow tumour cells that resist treatment one cell at a time, and suggests a timing window for combining drugs. The authors state it is only a proof of concept in cultured cells and human tissue sections, with no in vivo testing, and that the combination results are descriptive and need independent replication.

papers.abstract: Intratumour heterogeneity allows a fraction of cancer cells to escape otherwise effective treatment. Here we ask whether metabolic priming can recruit heterogeneous tumour cells into a transient mitochondrial state that is selectively vulnerable to photodynamic damage. Tetramethylrhodamine methyl ester (TMRM) has previously been shown to act as a mitochondria targeted photosensitizer; we exploit its voltage-dependent accumulation and dynamic fluorescence during pulsed illumination to quantify vulnerability in single cells. The response is a reproducible fluorescence excursion, a rise to a maximum followed by a decay, accompanied by reactive oxygen species production. Comparing seventeen descriptors of this excursion against subsequent fate in 195 cells across four arms shows that quantities referenced to each cell's own resting value outperform static intensity. The simple difference Fmax F0 predicts death with held-out areas under the curve of approximately 0.75 to 0.79, whereas resting intensity alone carries little transferable information and time to peak does not discriminate fate in the datasets tested. Metabolic priming with the PKM2 activator TEPP46 or with ethyl pyruvate increases the fraction of responding cells; under TEPP46 almost the whole population enters the responding state. PKM2 abundance is associated with faster entry into that state, and PKM2 is heterogeneous in human skin tumour sections. Four hours of camptothecin shifts the response distribution, increasing the fraction of cells above the untreated median from 50% to 76%, identifying a candidate intervention window. In combination experiments, TMRM photodynamic treatment produced survival below the Bliss-independence expectation with camptothecin or TRAIL, in both treatment orders and across three cell lines; these combination measurements are descriptive and require independent replication. The study therefore identifies a perturbation-revealed mitochondrial vulnerability that can be pharmacologically recruited and followed dynamically at single-cell resolution. It is a proof of concept in cultured cells and human tumour sections and has not been tested in vivo.

papers.title: Adjuvant myeloperoxidase inhibition promotes B and T cell mediated control of murine melanoma metastasis
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768197 v1

summary.background:
- Metastasis: cancer cells leaving a primary tumor and forming new tumors in distant organs.
- Myeloid cells: a family of white blood cells, including neutrophils, that the paper says can suppress immune attacks on tumors.
- Myeloperoxidase (MPO): an enzyme found in myeloid cells; the paper treats it as a drug target.
- Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs): web-like strands of DNA and proteins released by neutrophils; the paper proposes them as a downstream mediator of MPO's effect.
- B and T cells: adaptive immune cells that can attack tumors; the study shows the MPO inhibitor's effect depends on them.
- Adjuvant therapy: treatment given after the main tumor is removed or controlled, aimed at preventing recurrence or spread.
- Spontaneous model: mice that develop tumors on their own rather than from injected cancer cells.
summary.one_liner: In an immunocompetent mouse model of spontaneous melanoma, adjuvant myeloperoxidase (MPO) inhibition reduced multi-organ metastasis in a manner dependent on B, CD8+ and CD4+ T cells and linked to reduced neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) release, with similar effects reported in a spontaneous breast cancer model.
summary.plain: Melanoma is a skin cancer that spreads to distant organs, and that spread causes most deaths from it. This study tested whether blocking an enzyme called myeloperoxidase, which is made by a type of immune cell, could slow that spread in mice with a natural form of melanoma. The authors report fewer spread tumors across several organs, more B and T immune cells in the affected tissue, and fewer tumor cells circulating in the blood.
summary.why: Most current immune-directed cancer treatments do not target the myeloid cells that the authors say help metastasis, so an enzyme that can be blocked by a drug is a potentially new angle. The text does not establish that this approach works in patients, and the mouse results would need clinical testing before any conclusions about treatment.

papers.abstract: Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from primary tumors to distant organs and accounts for the majority of melanoma deaths, with a 5-year survival rate of only 30%. Despite strong evidence that myeloid cells promote metastasis, there are limited clinically effective myeloid-directed therapies. Here, we demonstrate that targeting myeloperoxidase (MPO), a myeloid-lineage restricted enzyme, significantly reduced multi-organ metastatic burden using an immunocompetent mouse model of spontaneous melanoma. Adjuvant MPO inhibition remodeled the metastatic microenvironment by a reduction in Ly6G+Ly6C+ myeloid cells and enrichment of B and T cell populations. Importantly, adjuvant MPO inhibitor-mediated metastatic control was dependent upon B, CD8+ T cells and CD4+ T cells, and rapidly reduced circulating and disseminated tumor cells. MPO inhibition markedly decreased NET release, while NET deficiency and inhibition recapitulated the anti-metastatic effects of targeting MPO, implicating NETs as a potential downstream mediator of MPO-driven metastasis. We further validated these findings in a distinct spontaneous breast cancer model where adjuvant MPO inhibition similarly reduced multi-organ metastatic burden with comparable changes within the metastatic immune microenvironment. Collectively, our studies introduce MPO as a druggable regulator of metastasis where MPO inhibition limits metastatic disease by targeting immunosuppressive myeloid cells.

papers.title: A KRASG12D-based organoid model for early oncogenic transformation of the mammary epithelium
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.766834 v1

summary.background:
- Organoids: small 3D clusters of cells grown in a dish that mimic some features of a real organ.
- KRAS: a gene that normally helps control cell growth; the G12D change is a common cancer-linked mutation that keeps it switched on.
- Cre-mediated expression: a genetic switch that turns a gene on in selected cells.
- Lumen: the hollow central cavity that normal mammary ducts and organoids form.
- Heterotypic organoid: an organoid containing a mix of two cell types, here mutant and normal cells.
- Apoptosis: programmed cell death, a normal way cells are removed.
- The study is a model-building paper in mice-derived cells; it does not test treatments in patients.
summary.one_liner: A mouse mammary (breast) epithelial organoid model in which Cre-induced KRASG12D expression produces neoplastic growth without lumen formation, with heterotypic competition between mutant and wild-type cells and suppressed apoptosis.
summary.plain: Researchers wanted a lab system for watching the very first steps of cancer forming in breast tissue. They grew small 3D clusters of healthy mouse mammary cells (organoids) and switched on a cancer-linked mutation, KRASG12D, in some of them. The mutated clusters grew abnormally and failed to form the hollow central space that normal ones develop, and mutant cells gained ground over normal neighbors.

papers.abstract: Modeling cancer initiation, progression, and metastasis has greatly impacted our understanding of fundamental cell and molecular mechanisms driving disease and has led to breakthrough treatments that greatly improve patient outcomes. Understanding the earliest stages of tumor formation is particularly important for uncovering the root causes of oncogenic transformation and tumor evolution. It has been historically difficult to model the cellular dynamics that drive the earliest stages of tumor evolution, largely due to difficulties in culturing and manipulating normal primary cells in 3-dimensional environments, triggering oncogenesis, and observing the resulting effects. Recent advances in 3D organoid culture provide a promising avenue to address these challenges. In this study, we have developed a Kras based organoid model of early tumorigenesis. In our model, oncogenic transformation was triggered by Cre-mediated expression of oncogenic KRASG12D in otherwise healthy murine-derived mammary epithelial organoids. While normal organoids displayed controlled organoid growth and morphogenesis, induction of KRASG12D caused neoplastic organoid growth that occurred with the absence of lumen formation. Gene expression analysis revealed up regulation of several KRAS effectors, and a broad repertoire of genes associated with tumor development and human breast cancer. Induction of oncogenic Kras in our model resulted in heterotypic organoids that possessed KRASG12D + cells growing alongside KRASG12D- cells. In this context, amplification of KRASG12D + cells occurred at the expense of KRASG12D- cells. Finally we observed that neoplastic growth of KRASG12D expressing organoids was associated with a suppression of apoptosis. We believe that our organoid model provides a platform that is suitable to examine the earliest stages of tumor development and can be expanded to study several questions related to cancer biology, prevention studies, therapeutic development, and beyond.

papers.title: The tumor suppressor role of the KRAS proto-oncogene in metastatic pancreatic cancer.
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767567 v1

summary.background:
- KRAS is a gene that normally helps control cell growth; mutated versions drive many cancers, and pancreatic cancer is among the most affected.
- A "proto-oncogene" is a normal gene that can become cancer-promoting; a "tumor suppressor" normally holds cancer back.
- Loss of heterozygosity (LOH) means a cell loses one of its two copies of a gene, here the normal KRAS copy.
- Interferons are signaling proteins that alert the immune system; CD8+ T cells are immune cells that kill tumor cells.
- Genetically engineered mouse models, lineage tracing (following cells' descendants over time), single-cell RNA sequencing, and orthotopic transplants (implanting cancer cells into the same organ in mice) are the main tools used.
- TBK1 and IRF are signaling molecules in the interferon pathway.
summary.one_liner: In a mouse model of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, loss of the wild-type Kras allele during tumor progression is linked to metastasis, poorer survival, reduced interferon signaling and CD8+ T cell infiltration, and tumors lacking the wild-type allele form only in immune-competent hosts when the wild-type allele is absent, suggesting wild-type KRAS acts as a tumor suppressor.
summary.plain: Most cancers with a KRAS mutation keep one normal copy and one mutated copy of the gene. As tumors spread, they often lose the normal copy, leaving only the mutant one. This study tracked that loss in mice and in patient samples, and found that tumors missing the normal copy spread more, were harder for the immune system to attack, and lost a key immune-alarm signal called the interferon response.
summary.why: It challenges the common view that KRAS works only as a cancer-driving oncogene, suggesting the normal copy may restrain tumors by helping immune cells find them. If confirmed, loss of the normal copy could serve as a marker of how aggressive a tumor is or of whether immune-based treatments might work, but the text alone does not show clinical implications.

papers.abstract: KRAS is the most frequently mutated proto-oncogene in human cancers. Progression to advanced disease is frequently associated with allelic imbalance of the KRAS locus with gain of the mutant allele and loss of the wild-type allele through clonal and sub-clonal loss of heterozygosity (LOH). While a large body of literature has focused on the effects of allelic imbalance on oncogene addiction through gain of the mutant allele, the role of the wild-type KRAS proto-oncogene in malignant progression has not been fully elucidated. To capture this phenomenon, we developed a first-in-class somatic mosaic and lineage tracing genetically engineered mouse model (smGMLT) of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma allowing for real time in vivo tracing of Kras-LOH. Longitudinal characterization of the smGMLT demonstrated the presence of a strong evolutionary bottleneck towards the selective loss of the wild-type allele at metastatic sites. Cross species analysis leveraging research autopsies and surgical specimens revealed that KRAS-LOH is associated with metastatic dissemination and shorter overall survival. Transcriptomic analysis through single-cell RNA sequencing uncovered a conserved phenomenon whereby KRAS-LOH is paralleled by an immune evasive phenotype through loss of the tumor-cell interferon response and reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration. In line with this evidence, orthotopic transplants of isogenic tumor populations differing for the Kras allelic status demonstrated that only cancer cells with Kras-LOH are are able to form tumors in immune competent animals. Restoration of the wild-type allele abrogates tumorigenesis in KrasLOH transplants in immunocompetent through activation of the TBK1-IRF axis. Altogether, these studies demonstrate that the KRAS proto-oncogene is a functional tumor suppressor in pancreatic cancer exerting its function through interferon-mediated, cell-extrinsic modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment.

papers.title: Spatial organization of a SPINK1-associated tumor-stromal ecosystem links metabolic remodeling to immune restriction in bladder cancer
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767479 v1

summary.background:
- Bladder cancer (BLCA): a cancer of the bladder lining.
- Tumor microenvironment: the non-cancer cells and tissue around a tumor, such as fibroblasts (supporting connective-tissue cells) that can be reprogrammed by cancer.
- Spatial transcriptomics: a method that measures which genes are active at specific locations in a tissue slice, so neighborhoods can be identified.
- SPINK1: a secreted protein found at high levels in some tumor cells here; the paper tests it in mice.
- Metabolic reactions: chemical conversions cells use for energy and building materials; lactate and glutamine are nutrients or byproducts that cells exchange.
- Reductive carboxylation and fatty acid synthesis: pathways by which cells build fats from glutamine-derived molecules.
- T cells and exhaustion: immune cells that lose effectiveness after prolonged exposure to tumors; CD8 T cells are cytotoxic killers.
- PD-1 blockade: an immunotherapy that releases a brake on T cells.
- Note: several links (metabolic circuit, ammonia handling, chemokine signaling) are predicted or associative in the abstract, not directly shown.
summary.one_liner: A spatial transcriptomics-based study identifying a SPINK1-high tumor epithelial and TPM2-high cancer-associated fibroblast niche in bladder cancer, linking proposed lactate-glutamine metabolic exchange to T-cell restriction and PD-1 blockade response in mice.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how bladder cancer cells and the supporting tissue around them (fibroblasts) work together in specific neighborhoods of a tumor, and how that teamwork may help the tumor avoid the immune system. The authors mapped these neighborhoods using spatial gene-activity data and computer-predicted metabolic flows, then tested the gene SPINK1 in mice. In those mice, removing Spink1 slowed tumor growth, brought in more killer T cells, and improved response to PD-1 immunotherapy.
summary.why: Bladder cancer immunotherapy does not work for everyone, so a candidate target that could be combined with PD-1 blockade is of interest. The metabolic and spatial links are mostly inferred from computer predictions and correlations, so they remain hypotheses that need direct experimental confirmation.

papers.abstract: Spatially organized tumor-stromal interactions contribute to metabolic remodeling and immune suppression in bladder cancer (BLCA). Using spatial transcriptional programs to define single-cell states, we identified a niche comprising SPINK1-high epithelial cells (E2) and TPM2-high cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) (C1). SPINK1 promoted tumor growth and myofibroblastic CAF programs, with EGFR and TGF-{beta} signaling implicated in tumor-CAF communication. Inferred metabolic reactions and spatial metabolite distributions supported a candidate circuit linking tumor-derived lactate to CAF oxidative metabolism and glutamine provision, followed by tumor glutamine utilization for reductive carboxylation and fatty acid synthesis. SPINK1 perturbation altered extracellular glutamine and lactate concentrations. Predicted chemokine interactions implicated C2/C3 CAFs in T cell recruitment, whereas the E2-C1 niche exhibited checkpoint and exhaustion-associated features. RHCG-positive tumor regions contained higher proportions of TOXCXCR4 cells among CD3 T cells, suggesting a possible association between ammonia handling and T cell dysfunction. In vivo, Spink1 loss attenuated tumor progression, increased cytotoxic CD8 T-cell infiltration, and enhanced tumor control during PD-1 blockade. These findings identify a spatially organized tumor-stromal niche associated with metabolic cooperation and immune restriction, supporting SPINK1 as a candidate therapeutic target in combination with immunotherapy.

papers.title: Glioblastoma exhibits bidirectional adaptation to treatment through JARID2-associated developmental plasticity
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.766938 v1

summary.background:
- Glioblastoma: the most common and aggressive primary brain tumour in adults; standard care is surgery, radiation and chemotherapy, and tumours usually recur.
- Transcriptional reprogramming: a change in which genes a cell switches on or off, without changing the DNA sequence itself.
- Bulk vs single-cell sequencing: bulk measures the average activity of a whole tumour sample; single-cell measures each cell separately.
- Polycomb / JARID2: protein complexes that add chemical marks to chromatin (DNA packaged with proteins) to keep developmental genes silenced.
- Bivalent chromatin: a mark combining both "on" and "off" signals at a gene promoter, often seen at developmental genes that are poised to be activated.
- Tumour microenvironment: the non-cancer cells and tissue surrounding the tumour cells.
- Abstract only: the text given is a short summary, so methods, sample sizes and statistics are not available to check.
summary.one_liner: Using longitudinal bulk and single-cell glioblastoma datasets, the authors define a JARID2 Binding Site (JBS) gene-expression axis that tracks how tumours shift from primary to recurrent states after standard chemoradiation, and link this shift to bivalent chromatin marks at neurodevelopmental genes.
summary.plain: Glioblastoma is an aggressive brain cancer that often returns after standard treatment, and the tumour's genetic activity changes in ways that are hard to predict from the first biopsy. This paper describes a scoring scheme, the JBS axis, based on a set of genes that positions tumours and individual cells along a line, and shows that recurrent tumours tend to move toward opposite ends of that line. The authors report that changes in the surrounding tumour environment shape this movement more than chemoradiation alone does.
summary.why: It offers a way to describe why treated glioblastoma can change in different directions, which matters because treatment choices may depend on that direction. The text suggests a link to Polycomb regulation (a system that keeps genes switched off during development) as a possible therapeutic target, but this is a proposal from the abstract and has not been tested in the text provided.

papers.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) exhibits bidirectional transcriptional reprogramming following standard-of-care (SoC) treatment, yet the direction cannot be predicted from primary tumours. Using independent longitudinal bulk and single-cell datasets, we show that this response is captured by a framework, the JARID2 Binding Site (JBS) axis. Tumours and cells can be positioned along this axis according to expression of JBS genes, with responder subtypes defined by movement along the axis from primary to recurrent states. The JBS axis aligns with established GBM ecosystems and their constituent cell populations, and recurrent tumours polarise towards opposite ends. Changes in tumour microenvironment composition strongly influence this polarisation and drive adaptive transcriptional responses more profoundly than chemoradiation alone. Mechanistically, JBS genes are enriched for promoters marked by persistent bivalent chromatin and neurodevelopmental regulatory programmes. These findings suggest that JARID2-associated Polycomb regulation maintains a reservoir of developmental plasticity that enables treatment-driven ecosystem adaptation and represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

papers.title: Connexin43 drives mitochondrial biogenesis and organelle stress in BRAF-mutant melanoma cells
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767001 v1

summary.background:
- BRAF is a gene whose mutation drives many melanomas; BRAF and MEK inhibitors are drugs that block its signalling pathway.
- Connexin43 is a protein that forms channels between cells and was previously described here as acting as a tumour suppressor.
- Mitochondria are the cell's energy-producing compartments; oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) is their main energy-making chain, with complexes such as CI, CIV and CV as parts of it.
- Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are chemically reactive oxygen molecules that can damage cells at high levels.
- DRP1 is a protein that splits mitochondria into fragments; mTORC1 is a growth-signalling pathway that regulates cell metabolism.
- The unfolded protein response is a cell stress program triggered when proteins fold improperly in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
- Experiments are cell-culture studies; the text does not report animal or patient data.
summary.one_liner: In BRAF-mutant melanoma cells, raising the gap-junction protein connexin43 boosts mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation and reactive oxygen species, while BRAF/MEK inhibitor treatment largely reverses these mitochondrial changes but not Cx43's sensitising effect.
summary.plain: Skin cancer cells with a common BRAF mutation often survive drug treatment by changing how their energy-producing structures, the mitochondria, work. This study looked at whether a protein called connexin43, which the same group had previously linked to better drug response, reshapes those mitochondria. The authors found that more connexin43 led to more mitochondria and more energy and oxidative stress, but that these changes were not what made the cells more responsive to the drugs.
summary.why: It suggests that mitochondrial stress and the mTORC1 signalling pathway could be possible targets for future cancer treatments, though the text only flags them for further investigation. It also shows that a link between a protein and drug response does not necessarily run through the mitochondria, which matters for interpreting such results.

papers.abstract: Metabolic flexibility helps cancer cells survive targeted therapy, and BRAF-mutant melanoma rewires mitochondrial metabolism in response to BRAF/MEK inhibitors (BRAF/MEKi). We previously showed that connexin43 (Cx43) acts as a tumour suppressor in BRAF-mutant melanoma and enhances the response to BRAF/MEKi. Here, we investigated whether mitochondrial remodelling contributes to these effects. Cx43 upregulation promoted mitochondrial biogenesis including selective increase of CI and CV, enhanced oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, alongside DRP1-associated mitochondrial fragmentation. Despite enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and OXPHOS, Cx43 upregulation was associated with respiratory chain remodelling, characterised by loss of complex IV, increased ER and mitochondrial stress, and enhanced mTORC1-associated signalling. These changes were accompanied by an adaptive unfolded protein response that did not engage the pro-apoptotic ATF4-CHOP axis. Notably, BRAF/MEK inhibition largely attenuated the mitochondrial biogenesis phenotype and most of the stress markers associated with Cx43 upregulation, while promoting mitochondrial network elongation and markedly increasing mitochondrial ROS. Despite this impact, Cx43-expressing tumour cells retained higher membrane potential, ROS levels and survival under glucose-limiting conditions. Collectively, these findings reveal a dissociation between the mitochondrial effects of Cx43 and its enhancement of the response to BRAF/MEKi, highlighting the complexity of Cx43-mediated metabolic regulation in BRAF-mutant melanoma. By distinguishing mitochondrial remodelling from therapeutic sensitisation, this study provides new insights into the response to BRAF/MEK inhibition and highlights mTORC1-associated signalling and mitochondrial oxidative stress as potential therapeutic vulnerabilities for further investigation.

papers.title: B7-H3 Orchestrates Fibro-Immune Spatial Organisation in Pancreatic Cancer
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.762837 v1

summary.background:
- PDAC: the most common form of pancreatic cancer, usually diagnosed late and rarely responsive to treatment.
- Desmoplastic stroma: the dense, fibrous scar-like tissue that surrounds many pancreatic tumours and can block immune cells.
- Immune checkpoint: a molecule that can switch off immune responses; drugs targeting these are a major cancer therapy approach.
- B7-H3 (CD276): a checkpoint-type molecule being studied as a drug target in pancreatic cancer trials.
- Spatial profiling: measuring molecules while keeping track of where each cell sits in the tissue.
- Neoadjuvant: treatment given before surgery to shrink a tumour.
- Single-cell analysis: examining the features of individual cells rather than averaging across a tissue sample.
summary.one_liner: A multiscale spatial profiling study of treatment-naive resected human pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) that maps B7-H3 (CD276) expression across regional and single-cell contexts and proposes it as a spatial organiser linked to a fibro-inflammatory, immunosuppressive tumour state, with a similar state reported in neoadjuvant (pre-surgery treated) samples.
summary.plain: Pancreatic cancer is very hard to treat, partly because the tissue around the tumour is dense with scar-like support cells and immune cells that fail to fight it. This study looked at where a molecule called B7-H3 sits within pancreatic tumour tissue, both in broad regions and in individual cells. The authors report that B7-H3 may help shape how tumour, support and immune cells are arranged, and that this pattern is linked to poorer outcomes.
summary.why: B7-H3 is already being tested in early-phase clinical trials for pancreatic cancer, so understanding its role in the tissue layout could inform how those treatments are interpreted. The text does not establish causation, and it is only a description of tissue patterns in a limited set of samples, so the findings are best read as hypothesis-generating.

papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most lethal cancers in the western world and is largely resistant to treatment. A major barrier to effective treatment is the highly desmoplastic and immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment, where the organisation of tumour, stromal and resident immune cells limit immune infiltration. B7-H3 (CD276) is an emerging immune checkpoint marker investigated in phase I and Ib/2 clinical trials in PDAC, yet its biological role within the tumour environment remains poorly understood. We performed an integrated multiscale spatial profiling study to map B7-H3 expression across regional and single-cell spatial contexts in treatment-naive resected human PDAC. Furthermore, we explored the B7-H3 landscape in the neoadjuvant setting. Our results demonstrate that B7-H3 is not simply overexpressed in cancer but may act as a spatial organiser of the PDAC microenvironment, associated with a transition from epithelial-intrinsic tumour architecture to fibro-inflammatory immune states that underpin immune suppression, aggressive disease and poor prognosis. This fibro-inflammatory state appears conserved within the neoadjuvant landscape.

papers.title: ERM proteins antagonistically control cancer invasion and metastasis via mechanosensing regulation
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767111 v1

summary.background:
- Metastasis: the spread of cancer from its original site to other organs.
- ERM proteins: ezrin, radixin and moesin, which connect the cell's internal scaffold (actin) to its membrane.
- Focal adhesions: anchor points where a cell grips the surrounding matrix.
- Focal adhesion kinase (FAK): an enzyme that signals inside the cell when adhesions form and mature.
- Mechanosensing: how cells detect and respond to physical forces such as pulling and stiffness.
- Anchorage dependence: normal cells need to be attached to a surface to grow; metastatic cells often lose this need.
- Contractility: the cell's internal pulling force generated by its actin and myosin network.
- Models used: matched low- and high-metastatic breast cancer cell lines, with lung metastasis tested in animals.
summary.one_liner: In breast cancer cell models, the ERM proteins (ezrin, radixin, moesin) act as antagonistic regulators of invasion and lung metastasis, with ezrin promoting and radixin or moesin restraining these traits through effects on focal adhesions and cellular force transmission.
summary.plain: Cancer spreads when cells break away from a tumour, move through tissue, and form new tumours elsewhere, such as in the lungs. This study looked at three related proteins, ezrin, radixin and moesin, that link a cell's internal skeleton to its outer surface. The authors found that all three were raised in the more spreading breast cancer cells, yet removing ezrin reduced invasion and lung spread in their models, while removing radixin or moesin increased them.
summary.why: The paper suggests that these proteins help cancer cells sense and pull on their surroundings, and that the balance among the three may act as a checkpoint for spread. The text is only an abstract, so the size and generality of the effect are not clear from it; it may matter for thinking about mechanical targets in metastasis, but that link is a possibility rather than a demonstrated outcome.

papers.abstract: Metastasis requires cancer cells to overcome anchorage dependence and rewire mechanosensing pathways. Here, we identify the ERM proteins ezrin, radixin, and moesin as key but antagonistic regulators of breast cancer metastasis. Expression profiling across matched low- and high-metastatic breast cancer models revealed consistent upregulation of all three ERM proteins in highly metastatic cells. Despite this, ezrin depletion reduced colony formation, invasion, and lung metastasis, whereas radixin or moesin depletion enhanced these phenotypes. Loss of radixin or moesin increased ezrin localization at the cell edge, while ezrin depletion reduced membrane-associated moesin, indicating a dynamic balance among ERM proteins. Ezrin depletion also increased focal adhesion size and number, FAK activation, and force transmission to the extracellular matrix, whereas radixin or moesin silencing produced opposite effects. Cellular force magnitude was inversely correlated with invasion, and pharmacological modulation of contractility reverted the effects of ERM depletion. These findings reveal an ERM-dependent mechanosensing checkpoint that regulates metastasis through control of adhesion dynamics and force transmission.

papers.title: A thermoreversible hydrogel model for in situ and ex situ analysis of tumor-immune interactions
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.766807 v1

summary.background:
- Immunotherapy: treatments that boost the patient's own immune system to attack cancer.
- CD8+ T cells: immune cells that can directly kill cancer cells.
- Spheroids: small 3D clusters of cells grown in the lab that mimic parts of a tumour.
- Hydrogel: a water-rich gel that holds cells in a scaffold, similar to a soft, jelly-like environment.
- Matrigel: a common gel extracted from animal tumour material; its composition varies between batches.
- Thermoreversible: the gel turns liquid or solid with temperature changes, so cooling can release the embedded cells.
- Metabolic profiling: measuring small molecules such as lactate and amino acids to see how cells are fuelling themselves.
- Flow cytometry: a method that counts and characterises individual cells by their surface and internal markers.
summary.one_liner: A defined, thermoreversible synthetic polyisocyanopeptide hydrogel is used as a 3D co-culture system for melanoma spheroids and primary CD8+ T cells, enabling in situ imaging and rapid cold-based cell recovery for metabolic and flow cytometry analysis.
summary.plain: Immunotherapy works for many cancer patients but not all, so scientists want lab models where tumour cells and immune cells can be studied together in three dimensions. This paper describes a lab gel made from a defined synthetic material, rather than a biologically derived mix like Matrigel, in which skin-cancer clusters and immune T cells are grown together. The authors report that the T cells survived and moved through the gel, that tumour cells showed more cell death during co-culture, and that cooling the gel released nearly all the cells in under 3 minutes for further testing.
summary.why: Reproducible, chemically defined culture systems could make it easier to compare how immune cells behave and what they do to tumours, which is relevant to understanding treatment response. The text is a summary of a study design and early measurements; its wider relevance to patient outcomes or clinical use is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Despite the clinical success of cancer immunotherapy, many patients fail to respond or develop resistance, highlighting the need to understand how interactions between tumor and immune cells influence treatment outcomes. Three-dimensional in vitro models allow these interactions to be studied under controlled conditions. However, Matrigel and other biologically derived scaffolds can vary in composition, offer limited independent control over matrix properties, and require cell-recovery procedures that complicate downstream analysis. Here, we present a co-culture model of melanoma spheroids and primary CD8+ T cells based on a defined, thermoreversible synthetic polyisocyanopeptide (PIC) hydrogel. PIC supported T cell viability and migration, with mean motility parameters similar to those in Matrigel and lower variability between experiments. Fluorescence imaging revealed CD8+ T cell infiltration and increased melanoma-cell apoptosis during co-culture. Cooling enabled recovery of nearly all embedded cells in less than 3 min without chemical or enzymatic matrix digestion. Metabolic profiling of recovered T cells identified time-dependent changes in intracellular lactate, amino acids, and tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, alongside changes in extracellular metabolite availability. Flow cytometry distinguished T cell populations with different effector profiles, with higher expression of effector markers in the fraction associated with melanoma spheroids. By combining a defined synthetic matrix with in situ imaging and rapid recovery for ex situ analysis, this model connects the spatial dynamics of tumor-immune interactions with metabolic and immune phenotypes, providing a basis for studies of immune-cell function and responses to immunotherapy.

papers.title: Recurrent astrocyte transcriptional states with spatial and functional specialization are induced by brain metastases independently of their primary tumor origin
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766881 v1

summary.background:
- Astrocytes are star-shaped support cells of the brain; "reactive" astrocytes change state in response to injury or disease.
- A "niche" is the local surrounding environment that a tumor depends on.
- Single-cell transcriptomics measures which genes are active in each cell; spatial transcriptomics also records where in the tissue each cell sits.
- Syngeneic models are mice with immune systems matched to the tumor cells, used to study cancer in a living animal.
- AP-1, STAT3 and HOPX are gene regulators or markers; AP-1 and c-FOS are involved in stress and inflammatory signaling.
- "Peritumoral interface" means the boundary zone around a tumor.
- Preprint-style claims on mouse models do not automatically carry over to human patients.
summary.one_liner: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics in syngeneic breast, lung and melanoma mouse models of brain metastasis identify recurrent, spatially organized astrocyte states, including an AST-BrM subset with AP-1-high and STAT3+/HOPX+-associated programs that were tested by genetic and pharmacological perturbation.
summary.plain: When cancer spreads to the brain, the nearby support cells called astrocytes change their behavior. This study mapped those changes in mice with breast, lung, or skin (melanoma) tumors that had spread to the brain, looking at individual cells and their locations in tissue. The authors report that a subset of these astrocytes changes specifically at the edge of the tumor, and that similar changes appear regardless of where the cancer started.
summary.why: Brain metastases are hard to treat, and the tissue around a tumor can help it grow. If the astrocyte programs described here hold up, they could point to new targets that act on the tumor's surroundings rather than the cancer cells alone. The text reports perturbation experiments and a link to clinical outcome, but the strength of these links cannot be judged from the abstract alone.

papers.abstract: Reactive astrocytes have emerged as important components of the brain metastasis niche, yet a state-resolved framework for metastasis-associated astrocyte biology is still lacking. Here, we integrate single-cell and spatial transcriptomics across syngeneic breast, lung and melanoma models of brain metastases to define a state-resolved astrocyte landscape. We identify recurrent tumor-associated astrocyte states shared across tumor origins, map their spatial distribution, and find that a subset, which we term AST-BrM, becomes selectively reprogrammed at the tumor-microenvironment interface, supporting niche-coupled organization rather than a diffuse brain-wide reactive response. AST-BrM defines distinct metastasis-associated astrocyte states at the peritumoral interface, distinguishes them from homeostatic-like astrocytes beyond generic inflammatory activation, and resolves into two therapeutically actionable programs: an AP-1-high axis and a STAT3+/HOPX+-associated axis. Genetic and pharmacologicall perturbations establish functional relevance, and an AP-1/c-FOS-driven signature is associated with clinical outcome. Together, these findings define conserved, spatially organized and actionable astrocyte programs that drive brain metastasis progression.

papers.title: mRNA-LNP vaccination induces microenvironment remodeling and generation of tissue-resident memory T cells in glioblastoma
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.11.762754 v1

summary.background:
- Glioblastoma: a fast-growing, usually fatal brain tumour that is hard to treat.
- Immunotherapy: treatments that use the body's own immune system to attack cancer.
- mRNA vaccine: a vaccine that delivers genetic instructions (messenger RNA) so cells make a target protein, here a tumour-specific mutant protein (EGFRvIII).
- Lipid nanoparticle (LNP): a fatty bubble that carries the mRNA into cells.
- T cells (CD4, CD8): immune cells that help coordinate or directly kill diseased cells.
- Tumour microenvironment: the mix of immune, support and blood-vessel cells surrounding a tumour.
- Spatial transcriptomics: measuring gene activity while keeping track of where each cell sits in the tissue.
- Tissue-resident memory T cells: long-lived immune cells that stay in an organ, here the brain, to guard against return of disease.
- Syngeneic model: mice whose immune system is intact and matched to the tumour cells, allowing immune responses to be studied.
summary.one_liner: In a mouse model of glioblastoma (EGFRvIII-driven, syngeneic), antigen-specific mRNA-LNP vaccination remodelled the tumour microenvironment and generated brain-resident memory CD8 T cells that provided long-term protection, with CXCL16-CXCR6 signalling highlighted as a possible driver.
summary.plain: Glioblastoma is an aggressive brain cancer that rarely responds to immune-based treatments. This study tested whether a vaccine made from messenger RNA, packaged in fatty nanoparticles, could train the immune system to fight a tumour in mice. The authors report that the vaccine cleared tumours, protected mice against new tumour challenges in the brain, and reshaped the immune environment around the tumour.
summary.why: The brain is hard to treat with immunotherapy, so a vaccine that leaves lasting immune memory inside the brain is of interest. The work is in mice only, and the text does not show whether these results would carry over to human patients; the proposed CXCL16-CXCR6 link is a correlation-based pathway analysis that would need direct testing.

papers.abstract: Glioblastoma remains highly refractory to immunotherapy, in part because of a profoundly immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment that limits effective T-cell responses. Although mRNA vaccines can induce anti-tumour immunity, how they reshape the glioblastoma immune ecosystem to support durable tumour control is not well understood. Here we use an immunocompetent EGFRvIII-driven syngeneic glioblastoma model and antigen-specific mRNA lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) vaccination to define the cellular and spatial mechanisms underlying therapeutic response. In our model, vaccination induced durable EGFRvIII-specific humoral and cellular immunity, resulting in complete tumour eradication and long-term protection against intracranial rechallenge. Integrative analyses incorporating flow cytometry, tumour interstitial fluid profiling, multiplex immunostaining, spatial transcriptomics and ligand-receptor modelling demonstrated extensive remodelling of the tumour microenvironment following vaccination. Early tumour control was associated with expansion of pro-inflammatory and antigen-presenting myeloid populations, increased cytotoxic CD8 T-cell infiltration and activation, enhanced interferon-responsive signalling, and the formation of immune-supportive spatial niches enriched for antigen presentation and chemokine-mediated cellular communication. Vaccination promoted inflammatory chemokine relay networks centred on the CXCL16-CXCR6 axis, a pathway linked to tissue residency programming in the central nervous system. Functional depletion studies identified CD4 and CD8 T cells as essential mediators of therapeutic efficacy, while durable protection was maintained by tumour-specific brain-resident memory CD8 T cells that persisted despite peripheral lymphocyte depletion. Together, these findings identify T-cell-driven microenvironmental remodelling as a critical mechanism linking mRNA vaccination to the establishment of long-term brain-resident anti-tumour immunity in glioblastoma.

papers.title: An expanded, phenotypically distinct tumor cell subset with low HPV mRNA increases recurrence risk
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.10.762907 v1

summary.one_liner: Single-cell RNA sequencing of HPV-positive oropharyngeal tumors and patient-derived xenografts identifies a phenotypically distinct HPV-low tumor cell subset whose pre-treatment size is associated with recurrence risk.
summary.plain:
Some tumors caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) in the throat come back after treatment, even though the virus is usually a sign of better response to therapy. This study looked at individual cancer cells and found a group of them that make little viral messenger RNA, the molecular copy used to make viral proteins. These cells appear more aggressive, and the share of them in a tumor before treatment was linked to a higher chance of recurrence.</plain>
<parameter name="why">The authors report that the size of the pre-treatment HPV-low fraction had a strong, independent association with recurrence, which suggests possible use as a clinical biomarker, though this is still an association and would need validation in other patients. It may also point to cell states that help tumors resist treatment, but the text does not show that these cells cause resistance.</why>
<parameter name="background">- HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer (throat cancer, mostly in the tongue base and tonsils) usually responds better to treatment than HPV-negative disease, but some cases recur.
- Patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) are human tumors grown in mice, used to test how tumors respond to drugs such as cisplatin.
- Single-cell mRNA sequencing measures which genes are active in each individual cell, revealing cell subgroups hidden in bulk tissue.
- mRNA is a short-lived copy of a gene used as a template for protein; "low HPV mRNA" means these cells express less of the viral genes.
- Senescence is a state where cells stop dividing; EMT (epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition) is a change that makes cells more mobile and invasive.
- Cell-cell interaction loss and "epithelial identity" refer to how cells stick together and retain their tissue-lining character.

papers.abstract: Human papillomavirus-related (HPV+) cancers harbor a subset of tumor cells expressing certain senescence-related transcripts and reduced levels of HPV mRNAs. We aimed to define this HPV-low population's biologic traits and clinical significance via integrated analysis of recurrence-prone human HPV+ oropharyngeal cancers (OPCs) and patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) of variable therapy sensitivity. Single-cell mRNA sequencing of PDXs and human tumors detected gene expression profiles in HPV-low cells indicating lack of senescence or terminal differentiation and intact tumorigenic capacity. HPV-low cells in cisplatin-refractory PDXs and particular human OPCs differentially upregulated multiple pathways linked to aggressive tumor biology, including RAS signaling, IL-6 signaling, and EMT. Predicted loss of cell-cell interactions among HPV-low cells reflected reduced epithelial identity, further supporting their more aggressive biology. Accordingly, the size of the pre-treatment HPV-low fraction had strong, independent association with recurrence risk. Genetic subclones within OPCs varied widely in content of HPV-low cells, which were enriched in particular lineages. Our findings uncover novel pro-tumor functions of HPV-low cells and support a central role for them in therapy resistance as well as potential utility as a clinical biomarker. Further elucidating mechanisms of cooperativity and plasticity between HPV-low and high states holds promise to reveal targets in treatment-refractory HPV+ malignancies.
